title: Bitcoin privacy upgrade and Solana speed create monitoring blind spots
summary: Developers are exploring Zcash-style shielded transactions for Bitcoin, and Solana is pushing toward 150-millisecond settlement finality. Alex and Jordan debate what both developments mean for transaction monitoring teams that weren't built for either. Plus: overdue obligations in Hong Kong and Korea that need attention now.
script:
ALEX: Let me put two stories on the table that arrived together this weekend, and I think the combination is more important than either story alone. Bitcoin developers are actively exploring shielded transaction capabilities, the kind Zcash built its entire value proposition around, without requiring a base-layer protocol change. And separately, Solana has reached a second public test network for 150-millisecond settlement finality. Jordan, my first reaction is that these are not really technology stories. They are transaction monitoring stories.

JORDAN: They are, and I'll tell you why I find the Bitcoin one more immediately concerning than most people are treating it. The Solana story is about speed. Uncomfortable, yes, but at least the chain is still visible. The Bitcoin shielded transaction story is about opacity, and it's being built at the layer where compliance teams actually do their work, which is on-chain analytics. Chainalysis, TRM, Elliptic, all of those tools are calibrated against Bitcoin's transparent UTXO model. If a second-layer shielded mechanism becomes viable at scale, that calibration breaks.

ALEX: I take that point, but I want to push back slightly on the urgency framing. The CoinDesk reporting describes this as developers actively exploring mechanisms. It is not live. It is not even in testnet. The regulatory community, including the Financial Action Task Force, has been building its virtual asset guidance precisely around the assumption that blockchains are transparent by default and privacy is the exception to manage. If this moves from research to deployment, that assumption holds until it doesn't.

JORDAN: And that's exactly where I'd push back on your regulatory optimism, Alex. Regulators build guidance around the world as it exists, not the world that's coming. By the time FATF updates Recommendation 15 guidance to address a Bitcoin shielded layer, the tooling gap will already exist. The compliance team at a Virtual Asset Service Provider licensed under MAS Notice SFA 04-N02, or under Hong Kong's Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, is the one sitting between the technology shift and the regulator catching up. That gap lands on the MLRO's desk, not on FATF's.

ALEX: Agreed on the gap. So let's talk about the Solana point as well, because 150 milliseconds is a genuinely different operating environment. Current transaction monitoring frameworks, even sophisticated ones, are built around the assumption that there is some latency between initiation and settlement. That latency is the window in which a VASP can screen, flag, hold, or escalate. At 150 milliseconds, that window is effectively gone for real-time intervention.

JORDAN: Right, and the industry has been through a version of this conversation with faster payment systems. The UK's Faster Payments, Australia's New Payments Platform, Singapore's FAST rails. The lesson from each of those was that you cannot lift a correspondent-banking monitoring model and apply it to instant settlement. You have to move the screening to pre-transaction controls. Name screening, velocity checks, wallet risk scoring, all of that has to happen before the transaction initiates, not after it clears.

ALEX: But here is where I think the Solana case is harder than those examples. With FAST or the New Payments Platform, the account infrastructure is still anchored to an institution with a Know Your Customer obligation. With a public blockchain at 150-millisecond finality, you have pseudonymous wallets, no mandatory pre-transaction screening requirement in most jurisdictions, and irreversible settlement. The travel rule under FATF Recommendation 16 requires originator and beneficiary information to accompany virtual asset transfers. At 150 milliseconds, the mechanics of collecting and transmitting that information in real time are not resolved.

JORDAN: They're not resolved, and I'll tell you what's sitting in my in-tray right now as a result. VASPs operating under the SFC's KYT framework in Hong Kong have a quarterly review obligation due for Know Your Transaction tooling effectiveness. That review is due at end of this quarter. If your KYT vendor hasn't been asked about their coverage of high-throughput chains, and specifically about what happens to hop-distance methodology and sanctioned-mixer flagging when settlement approaches real-time, that conversation needs to happen this week.

ALEX: So what should listeners do with both of these, before we move on?

JORDAN: Two specific things. First, if you are an MLRO or head of financial crime at a licensed VASP anywhere in Asia-Pacific, raise a formal question in writing to your KYT vendor this week asking how their tooling addresses near-real-time settlement chains and what their product roadmap covers for shielded transaction detection on Bitcoin second-layer constructions. Get it in writing so it's in your control environment record. Second, include both developments in your next quarterly risk assessment update. Regulators conducting thematic reviews, and the HKMA has been explicit about this in its supervisory priorities, will ask whether your risk framework anticipated emerging technology risks. Having documented that you identified these developments, and assessed their materiality for your book of business, is a defensible position. Not having done so is not.

ALEX: Moving on, a couple of overdue obligations deserve a direct mention. The HKMA issued a thematic review of Suspicious Transaction Report narrative quality across its supervised Authorized Institutions late last year, and deficiency letters went to roughly a quarter of the population. Closure of those findings is still listed as an active obligation, and we're now almost six months past the original due date. If your institution received a deficiency letter and you haven't formally closed the remediation, that is a live regulatory exposure.

JORDAN: And the language in those letters matters. The HKMA's Supervisory Policy Manual module on AML and counter-terrorist financing is explicit about what adequate STR narrative looks like: factual specificity, articulation of the suspicious indicator, connection to the customer's known risk profile. If your remediation plan just says you've run training, that's not closure. Closure means evidenced improvement in narrative quality across a sample of your recent STRs.

ALEX: And in Korea, VASPs that haven't completed their annual travel-rule compliance review under Article 5-2 of the Financial Transaction Reports Act are exposed to both the Korea Financial Intelligence Unit and the Financial Services Commission. That review window closed in March, and it's now September. If you're operating in the Korean market and this hasn't been signed off, treat it as urgent.

JORDAN: Before we close, the XRP Ledger's Batch transaction amendment slipping to October ninth is worth a brief note. Atomic bundling of multiple operations into a single ledger entry creates aggregation questions for transaction monitoring. If your volume on the XRP Ledger is material, confirm with your technology team that your monitoring system captures bundled transactions as constituent parts, not just as a single aggregated entry. A bundled transaction that clears a threshold only when disaggregated is a detection gap.

ALEX: One more item before we sign off. Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po expressed confidence this weekend that markets would respond positively to the Xi-Trump summit outcome. We note it only because geopolitical friction reduction tends to accelerate cross-border capital flows, which means compliance teams should be watching for volume spikes in correspondent channels and digital asset corridors in the coming weeks.

JORDAN: The full obligation register and source links for everything we've covered today are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. If your KYT tooling conversation with your vendor is on your to-do list from this episode, do it before Friday. Have a good Sunday.
